sections.markdown:
## C — Your driving privilege and other important information: the point system and suspension threshold, habitual traffic offender rules, occupational license limits, reinstatement, test accessibility, medical and invisible disability reporting, the free voting ID petition, seat belts and child seats, liability insurance, saving fuel, the driver education grant and organ donation
Knowledge domain: how a Wisconsin driver keeps or loses the driving privilege — points, habitual offender status, occupational licenses and reinstatement — plus the seat belt, child seat and insurance rules every licensed driver must follow and the DMV programs a new driver should know about.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Every driving record starts at zero points, and being convicted of a traffic law violation can add demerit points. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
Drivers holding a probationary license, only an ID card, or no license at all have their points doubled on the second conviction and every one after it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Collecting 12 or more demerit points within any 12-month period leads to suspension or revocation of your driving privilege. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
You become a habitual traffic offender with four or more major traffic violation convictions, or 12 or more minor ones, within five years. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
The DMV website lists the points for each violation and which violations count as major or minor. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
A habitual traffic offender's driving privilege is revoked for five years, with possible eligibility for an occupational license after a two-year wait. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
Your Wisconsin driving privilege can be lost through suspension, revocation, cancellation, disqualification or denial, even if you do not hold a Wisconsin license. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A01
To apply for an occupational license, first check your eligibility on the DMV website; you will need to show proof of financial responsibility. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A01
An occupational license caps your driving at 12 hours per day and 60 hours per week. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A01
Occupational license driving is limited to trips to and from work, school and places needed to maintain your household, such as the grocery store and medical appointments. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A01
An occupational license also covers trips to the agency handling your Intoxicated Driver Program (IDP) assessment and Driver Safety Plan (DSP). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A01
A revoked license can be reinstated once the revocation period ends, by presenting proof of identity, paying a reinstatement fee and, if required, filing proof of financial responsibility. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
The knowledge and signs tests can be taken with audio and in many languages, which are listed on the DMV website. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
You can tell the DMV about an invisible disability using the Invisible Disability Disclosure form MV2167, sent by email, mail or fax. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
An invisible disability disclosure is made available to law enforcement officers and WisDOT employees. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
Report any health condition that could affect your driving to the DMV, which you can do on the Wisconsin Driver License Application MV3001. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A02
Wisconsin citizens can get a free ID card for voting through a petition process using the ID Application MV3004 and the Administrator Petition for unavailable documents MV3012. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A02
Through the voting ID petition you receive a document you can use in time to vote. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A02
To start the voting ID petition process you must be at least 17 years old and a U.S. citizen. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A02
For the voting ID petition, bring whatever you have of proof of name and birth date, proof of identity, Wisconsin residency, proof of U.S. citizenship and your Social Security number. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A02
Wisconsin law requires the driver and all passengers of any age to wear seat belts. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A02
Seat belts keep you positioned to control the vehicle, help prevent injury in a crash and help keep you from being thrown out. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A02
Buckle your seat belt before you start driving and make sure every passenger buckles up too. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A02
You must still wear a seat belt in a vehicle that has air bags. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A03
The lap belt should sit snugly across your hip bones just below your stomach, and the shoulder belt should cross your chest. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
Adjust the belt so your fist fits between it and your chest, and never tuck the shoulder belt under your arm or let it hang loose over your arm. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A03
Generally, children ride in a child safety seat until age four and in a booster seat until age eight. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A03
Check the child safety seat's manual for how to fasten the seat belt and for its weight and height requirements. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A03
You must carry valid liability car insurance to drive in Wisconsin and show proof of it when a police officer asks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A03
Your insurance must come from a business approved in Wisconsin, though drivers from another state may show proof from their own state's insurer. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A03
When you drive someone else's car, it is your responsibility to make sure that car is insured. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A03
You can save fuel by carpooling, ride sharing, biking, taking the bus or walking, and by avoiding heavy traffic periods. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A03
Stop-and-go driving adds wear and tear, while slowing down gradually saves both fuel and brakes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A03
A vehicle in poor condition costs more to run and could break down and crash, and low tire pressure lowers fuel mileage. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A03
Under the Driver Education Grant Program, income-eligible teens can have their classroom training, behind-the-wheel training, or both paid for by the state [A03].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A03
People of all ages can register as organ and tissue donors, regardless of their health history. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A03
If you are 18 or older, your organ donor decision cannot be overridden by your family or anyone else, so share your decision with your family. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

Misconceptions: points are not just added up forever, the suspension trigger is reaching the threshold within a rolling year; you can lose a Wisconsin driving privilege without ever holding a Wisconsin license; an occupational license is not a full license and covers only work, school, household and treatment trips within daily and weekly hour caps; air bags do not replace seat belts; tucking the shoulder belt under your arm is wrong; borrowing a car does not shift the insurance duty to its owner alone.
Mnemonics: twelve points in twelve months means you are parked; four major or twelve minor in five years makes a habitual offender; the occupational license runs twelve a day and sixty a week; car seat to four, booster to eight; lap on the hips, shoulder on the chest, a fist of room.
Glossary: demerit points means points added to your record for traffic convictions; suspension means a temporary withdrawal of the driving privilege; revocation means a cancellation of the privilege that requires reinstatement; habitual traffic offender means a driver who reaches the major or minor conviction counts within five years; occupational license means a restricted license for essential trips; liability insurance means coverage for harm you cause to others.
Dynamic facts: the DMV website keeps the current lists of violation points, test languages and occupational license eligibility, and the driver education grant is described as a new program, so check those pages before relying on details.
